slides.title: White blood cell count (WBC)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · What it is used for · 1/2
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood (EDTA, purple-top tube)  ·  Units: ×10⁹/L, /µL

What it is used for: The test helps diagnose or monitor disorders with a high or low WBC: signs of infection (fever, chills, body aches, headache, a wound that is red, has pus or won’t heal, an ongoing cough), inflammation or autoimmune disease; and a disease or medicine that weakens the immune system — if the count gets too low, the provider may adjust treatment. Children may be tested as part of routine screening.

Physiology: White blood cells (leukocytes) are part of the immune system: made in the bone marrow and found in the blood and lymph tissue, they travel through the bloodstream and tissues to where they are needed to fight infections and other diseases. There are five major types — neutrophils, lymphocytes, monocytes, eosinophils and basophils; the WBC measures their total number.

slides.title: White blood cell count (WBC)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · What it is used for · 2/2
bullets: When you get sick, the body makes more white cells to fight bacteria, viruses or other foreign substances, raising the count. Some cancers, HIV (a virus that attacks white cells) and certain medicines such as chemotherapy lower it.

slides.title: White blood cell count (WBC)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Interpreting the result
bullets: High: Causes of leukocytosis (a high WBC) include infection, an inflammatory disease such as rheumatoid arthritis, allergy, leukemia or Hodgkin disease, and tissue damage from a burn or surgery. Smoking, stress, a reaction to a medicine or pregnancy can also raise the count.

Low: Causes of leukopenia (a low WBC) include bone marrow damage from infection, disease or treatments such as chemotherapy, cancers that affect the bone marrow, an autoimmune disorder such as lupus, and HIV.

slides.title: White blood cell count (WBC)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Pre-analytics and interferences · 1/2
bullets: Pre-analytics: No special preparation is needed, but some medicines may need to be stopped before the test, so tell the provider about everything you take. Do not stop any medicine unless the provider says so.
Adults give a sample from a vein. Newborns and young babies have a heel stick; older babies and children give blood from the fingertip or arm.

Per the WHO phlebotomy guidelines, hematology tests use an EDTA tube (usually purple top): EDTA removes calcium by forming calcium salts. The tube needs a full draw and gentle inversion so the blood mixes thoroughly with the additive — poor mixing can give erroneous results. Cap colors may differ by manufacturer.

Interferences: Diet, activity level, medicines, having a menstrual period, not drinking enough water and other factors can affect CBC results; an abnormal level does not always mean a condition that needs treatment.

slides.title: White blood cell count (WBC)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Pre-analytics and interferences · 2/2
bullets: Limitations: A WBC shows whether white cells are too high or too low but cannot confirm a diagnosis; it is usually done with a complete blood count, blood differential, blood smear and/or bone marrow test. The differential shows the amount of each type.

slides.title: Peripheral blood smear
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · What it is used for · 1/2
bullets: Specimen: Venous or fingertip capillary blood; heel stick in babies

What it is used for: For a blood smear, blood is spread on a glass slide and treated with a special stain; a laboratory professional then checks the size, shape and number of red cells, white cells and platelets under a microscope. Automatic computer programs may be used to help.

A blood smear alone can't diagnose a disease, but with other tests it helps diagnose and monitor blood and bone marrow disorders, certain cancers of the blood, bone marrow and lymphatic system, infections and certain parasites.

slides.title: Peripheral blood smear
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · What it is used for · 2/2
bullets: After an abnormal CBC, a smear confirms cell size and number and shows more about how the cells look, including their color. It is also ordered for symptoms of a blood-cell condition (fatigue, jaundice, unusual bleeding, easy bruising, fever, bone pain, swollen lymph nodes), to check treatment of anemia or blood cancer, and for flu-like symptoms in people living in or travelling to areas where malaria or babesiosis is common.

slides.title: Peripheral blood smear
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Interpreting the result
bullets: High: Results describe what the cells look like and how many there are, and anything else unusual, such as parasites. Abnormal red cells may be a sign of anemia, sickle cell disease, hemolytic anemia, thalassemia or bone marrow disorders; abnormal white cells of infection, leukemia or bone marrow disorders; abnormal platelets of thrombocytopenia, thrombocytosis or thrombocythemia.

slides.title: Peripheral blood smear
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Pre-analytics and interferences
bullets: Pre-analytics: No special preparation is needed, though fasting may be required if other tests are ordered. Blood is drawn from a vein, sometimes by finger prick, and from the heel in babies.
Interferences: Severe illness, stress and blood transfusions can also cause abnormal smear results.
Limitations: Smear results alone usually can't diagnose a condition: the provider combines them with history, symptoms and other tests and may order more tests to find the cause.

slides.title: Blast
slides.caption:
Refer to a physician / haematologist
Size: Large, 15–25 µm (lymphoblast)
Nucleus: Large, round, pale, fine chromatin; 1–5 nucleoli
Cytoplasm: Narrow dark-blue rim, clear zone around the nucleus
Granules: None
Key feature: Nucleoli + fine chromatin + very little cytoplasm.
Seen in: A blast is an immature blood cell; seen in blood films in leukaemia.
Schematic (not a photomicrograph)

slides.title: Leukaemia: definition and causes (Najmitdinov)
bullets: Leukaemia (“white-blood disease”) is a group of tumours growing from individual “roots” of the bone marrow. The name comes from the tumour first being found in the white-cell line; it was later shown that it can also arise in the red-cell and platelet lines.
The book gives erythromyelosis (Di Guglielmo disease) and erythraemia (Vaquez disease) as examples of this group; the term “leukaemia” is kept because it is so widespread in world literature.
It occurs in adults and in children.
The cause is not established: the book mentions virus, hereditary and radiation (ionizing radiation) theories; according to the author none of them has been confirmed.

slides.title: Classification of leukaemias (textbook, 1998)
bullets: The book divides leukaemias by course into acute and chronic forms.

Acute: undifferentiated-cell leukaemia (from reticular cells), haemocytoblastic, myeloblastic, monoblastic and lymphoblastic leukaemia, erythromyelosis (Di Guglielmo), megaloblastic and plasmoblastic leukaemia.

Chronic: chronic myeloid leukaemia, chronic lymphocytic leukaemia, myeloma (Rustitsky–Kahler disease), erythraemia (Vaquez), osteomyelosclerosis, chronic megakaryocytic leukaemia, lymphogranulomatosis (Hodgkin), Waldenström macroglobulinaemia.

slides.title: Pathogenesis of leukaemia: four features (Najmitdinov)
bullets: Hyperplasia: because of changes in genes, a young (blast) cell in one of the “roots” multiplies very fast and loses the ability to mature — a clone of pathological young cells forms in the marrow.
Metaplasia: the pathological clone crowds out normal blood formation; megakaryocytes die and platelets fall (haemorrhagic syndrome), and metaplastic anaemia develops.

Anaplasia: cytomorphological and chemical changes of leukaemic cells — the shape of nuclei and nucleoli and the number and structure of chromosomes change (for example the Philadelphia chromosome in chronic myeloid leukaemia).
Heterotopic foci: foci of blood formation appear in organs where blood is not normally made (skin, muscle, nerve fibres and others), causing pain and organ damage.
Consequences: reduced immunity, necrotic-inflammatory changes and infections, fever, bleeding and anaemia.

rows: ≥20% blasts in blood/bone marrow (with immunophenotype); in WHO-2022 this threshold is not required for many genetic types %

slides.title: Which of these, per the source, causes a LOW white count (leukopenia)?
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct: HIV attacks white cells and causes leukopenia.

Basis: HIV, bone marrow damage, cancers affecting the marrow and lupus cause leukopenia; infection and burns cause leukocytosis.

slides.title: The WBC is above normal. Does that alone confirm a diagnosis?
options: Yes, a high count confirms an infection
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct: it is read with a differential, smear and other tests.

Basis: A WBC shows whether the count is high or low but cannot confirm a diagnosis.

slides.title: Why order a blood smear for flu-like symptoms after travel to a malaria area?
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct: for example malaria or babesiosis parasites.

Basis: Parasites may be seen on the smear under the microscope.

slides.title: Leukemias, etiology, pathogenesis and classification?
bullets: 1. Leukemias are clonal neoplastic diseases of hematopoietic cells; they begin in the bone marrow and spill into the blood.

2. Etiology/risk factors: ionizing radiation, benzene, prior chemotherapy, genetic syndromes (Down), prior MDS/MPN; pathogenesis – genetic alterations (translocations, mutations), for example t(9;22) BCR::ABL1, t(15;17) PML::RARA.

3. Classification: acute (blasts predominate) and chronic (mature cells predominate); myeloid and lymphoid; the current standard is WHO 5th edition (2022) and ICC 2022: types defined genetically and by differentiation.
4. Diagnostic work-up: CBC and smear, bone marrow aspirate/trephine biopsy, cytochemistry, flow cytometry (immunophenotype), cytogenetics, FISH and molecular tests (PCR, NGS).

slides.title: Leukemias, etiology, pathogenesis and classification?
bullets: 5. In acute myeloid leukemia the classical threshold is ≥20% blasts in blood or bone marrow; in WHO-2022 this threshold has been removed for most genetically defined types.

slides.title: Acute leukemias. Bone marrow and peripheral blood picture in acute leukemias?
bullets: 1. Acute leukemia is clonal proliferation of immature blast cells and suppression of normal hematopoiesis.

2. Peripheral blood: anemia (normocytic), thrombocytopenia, leukocytes increased, normal or decreased; blasts (high nuclear/cytoplasmic ratio, fine chromatin, nucleoli); "leukemic hiatus" – no intermediate forms between blasts and mature cells.
3. Bone marrow: hypercellular, many blasts – ≥20% for AML (in some genetic types the threshold is lower/absent); normal lineages suppressed.
4. Identifying the myeloid type: Auer rods, myeloperoxidase positivity; in APL promyelocytes with many Auer rods and the risk of DIC – an emergency.
5. Confirmation: flow cytometry (myeloid/B/T lineage), cytogenetics and molecular tests (for example t(15;17) PML::RARA, FLT3, NPM1) – for classification and prognosis.
6. Remission: <5% blasts in the bone marrow, recovery of blood counts.

slides.title: Leukemias, etiology, pathogenesis, stages. Clinical diagnostic characteristics?
bullets: 1. Leukemias are clonal neoplasia of hematopoietic stem/progenitor cells; risk factors: radiation, benzene, cytostatics, inherited syndromes, prior MDS/MPN.
2. Pathogenesis: genetic damage (translocations – BCR::ABL1, PML::RARA; mutations – FLT3, NPM1, etc.) arrests differentiation and enhances proliferation; normal hematopoiesis is suppressed.
3. Stages (clinical course): initial, advanced (overt), remission (complete/partial), relapse, terminal; in CML chronic phase → accelerated → blast crisis.
4. Clinical diagnostic signs: anemic, hemorrhagic, infectious and hyperplastic (lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly) syndromes; in blood blasts, cytopenias or leukocytosis.
5. Diagnosis: CBC/smear → bone marrow → cytochemistry, immunophenotype, cytogenetics/molecular; classification by WHO-2022/ICC.
